item.title: Getting started with DVC: purpose, how it works, and the commands
item.author: nb@nbtyfood.com (jobcher)
item.description:
Datasets and model files do not belong in Git. A CSV of a few hundred megabytes, and a model larger than that, makes clone, diff, and rollback slow. DVC (Data Version Control) keeps those files outside Git, commits a small pointer instead, and uses the same idea for the training pipeline: when code, parameters, or data change, only the affected steps run again.

DVC does not replace Git. Git keeps the code and the pointers. DVC keeps the data, the models, and the pipeline outputs.

What it is for

Day to day, that is four jobs:

  • Version data and models. Each dvc add or pipeline rerun records a content hash that lines up with a Git commit.
  • Sync those large files between machines. One copy lives in the local cache, another on a remote (disk, NFS, S3, SSH, or WebDAV).
  • Turn “prepare data → train → write metrics” into a pipeline. Steps whose dependencies did not change are skipped.
  • Switch data and models together with the code. After git checkout, run dvc checkout.

Git LFS can also replace a large file with a pointer, and the blob storage is usually tied to the Git host. A DVC remote can be object storage or an SSH machine you already operate, and the pipeline is part of the tool: it records which dataset, which script, and which parameters a training run depended on.

How it works

The workspace, the local cache, and the remote each hold a copy of the data. Git holds only the pointers.

flowchart LR
  workspace["Data and models in the workspace"] -->|dvc add / dvc repro| cache["Local cache .dvc/cache"]
  cache -->|dvc push| remote["Remote"]
  remote -->|dvc pull| cache
  cache -->|dvc checkout| workspace
  meta[".dvc, dvc.yaml, dvc.lock"] -->|git commit| gitrepo["Git repository"]

Pointer files

dvc add data/raw.csv does three things: hash the file contents, store the file in .dvc/cache, write data/raw.csv.dvc beside it, and add data/raw.csv to .gitignore.

A pointer file looks like this (the hash and size are filled in by the command):

1outs:
2- md5: 22a1a2931c8370d3aeedd7183606fd7f
3  size: 1048576
4  hash: md5
5  path: raw.csv

The file is only a few lines, so it can be committed. After someone clones the repo they still do not have the CSV. dvc pull fetches the bytes from the remote by that hash.

Directories work the same way. dvc add data/ tracks the whole directory. The cache stores each file plus a directory listing.

Content-addressed storage

The cache lives in .dvc/cache and is stored by MD5 of the file contents, not by file name. Identical contents are stored once. Change one byte and the hash changes, so the cache gains a new object. The old object stays until you clean it up. Checking out an old commit restores the file as long as that hash is still in the cache or on the remote.

Workspace files are often hard links into the cache, and they are read-only, so editing the workspace does not overwrite a historical version in the cache. To change a tracked file, run dvc unprotect, edit it, then dvc add again.

A pipeline records dependencies

A pipeline is dvc.yaml. Each stage has:

  • cmd: the command to run
  • deps: inputs, data files or code
  • params: parameters read from params.yaml
  • outs: data or models the command writes; DVC caches these
  • metrics: a metrics file. With cache: false it stays out of the cache, and a small file can go straight into Git

dvc repro writes dvc.lock. The lockfile records the hash of every dependency and output from that run, and it should be committed. The next rerun compares the workspace with the hashes in the lock:

  • Dependencies, parameters, and the command are unchanged: skip the stage
  • An input to one stage changed: start at that stage and follow the graph downstream
  • Before a stage runs, DVC deletes the outs that stage declared, then runs cmd. The script has to create its output directories, and it should overwrite output files rather than append to them

dvc.yaml says what to do. dvc.lock says what the last run produced. Both go into Git. The CSV and model.pkl go into the cache and the remote.

If a metrics file sets cache: false, its hash is still written to dvc.lock and the file itself stays in the workspace. You can run dvc metrics diff and compare AUC across two commits without pulling the data.

Where configuration goes

dvc init creates .dvc/. Commit .dvc/config, which holds the remote URL. Write secrets to .dvc/config.local. That file is ignored by default.

One complete version is these four pieces:

Where What
Git Code, params.yaml, dvc.yaml, dvc.lock, *.dvc, .dvc/config
.dvc/cache Data and models, stored by hash
Remote A copy of the cache, so other machines can dvc pull
.dvc/config.local Credentials for the remote, not committed

Commands

The commands sit next to Git: one side commits pointers, the other pushes data.

Init and remotes

 1dvc init
 2
 3# Local disk or a shared mount. -d makes it the default remote
 4dvc remote add -d storage /mnt/dvc-storage
 5
 6# Object storage. Install the plugin first, and keep credentials in the local config
 7# pip install dvc-s3
 8dvc remote add -d storage s3://team-ml/churn/dvc
 9dvc remote modify --local storage access_key_id 'AKIA...'
10dvc remote modify --local storage secret_access_key '...'
11
12dvc remote list
13dvc remote default storage

An SSH remote is ssh://user@host/data/dvc-cache. Pick one remote for the team and commit its address in .dvc/config.

Synology WebDAV as DVC storage

When a Synology NAS is already on the home or office LAN, DSM’s WebDAV Server can be the DVC remote. Another machine then uses dvc pull to fetch the data and the model.

On the NAS:

  1. Install WebDAV Server from Package Center. Enable HTTPS and leave the port at the default 5006. On a LAN you can also enable HTTP on 5005.
  2. Control Panel → Shared Folder, and create a folder that holds only the cache, for example dvc. Turn the recycle bin off for that folder, so cleaning up old versions actually returns disk space.
  3. Control Panel → User & Group, and create a user dvc. Grant that user read/write on the shared folder, and allow WebDAV Server in the user’s application permissions.

In the project, install the WebDAV extra, commit the address, and keep the account on the machine:

1pip install 'dvc[webdav]'
2
3dvc remote add -d nas-webdav webdavs://192.168.1.20:5006/dvc
4dvc remote modify --local nas-webdav user 'your-user'
5dvc remote modify --local nas-webdav password 'your-password'

Replace 192.168.1.20 with the NAS address on the LAN. dvc is the shared folder name. For HTTP only, use webdav://192.168.1.20:5005/dvc.

DSM ships with a self-signed certificate. If dvc push fails on certificate verification, turn verification off for LAN use:

1dvc remote modify nas-webdav ssl_verify false

If the NAS already has your own certificate, or you exported the CA, point ssl_verify at that pem file.

What you commit is .dvc/config:

1[core]
2    remote = nas-webdav
3['remote "nas-webdav"']
4    url = webdavs://192.168.1.20:5006/dvc
5    ssl_verify = false

The account stays in .dvc/config.local, which is already ignored:

1['remote "nas-webdav"']
2    user = your-user
3    password = your-password

Push and check it like any other remote:

1dvc push
2dvc status --cloud

If dvc push fails while listing directories, enable Depth Infinity in WebDAV Server and push again. A reverse proxy in front of port 443 has to allow uploads larger than a single model file. The built-in 5006 port has no such limit.

Track data

1dvc add data/raw.csv          # write the .dvc file, cache the data, ignore the original
2dvc unprotect data/raw.csv    # make a read-only hard link writable before editing
3dvc add data/raw.csv          # refresh the hash after the edit
4dvc commit                    # copy workspace edits of tracked files back into the cache and update pointers
5dvc remove data/raw.csv.dvc   # stop tracking the file and update the ignore rules

Use dvc add for new data, or to update a file tracked by its own .dvc file. Leave pipeline outputs alone. Change a dependency and run dvc repro.

Sync and switch versions

1dvc status            # workspace compared with the pointers
2dvc status --cloud    # what the local cache is missing relative to the remote
3dvc push              # cache → remote
4dvc fetch             # remote → cache, workspace unchanged
5dvc pull              # fetch, then checkout
6dvc checkout          # restore the workspace from the cache using the pointers in the current Git commit

Switching code and switching data are two commands:

1git checkout <commit>
2dvc checkout

If the cache does not contain that hash, dvc checkout reports it missing. Run dvc pull next.

Pipelines

Write dvc.yaml by hand, or generate it with dvc stage add. This is the same train stage as in the example below:

1dvc stage add -n train \
2  -d src/train.py -d data/train.csv -d data/test.csv \
3  -p train \
4  -o models/model.pkl \
5  -M metrics.json \
6  python src/train.py

-M declares a metrics file. The default is cache: false.

1dvc repro                 # rerun stages whose dependencies changed, in graph order
2dvc repro train           # check train and its upstream stages only
3dvc repro --dry           # print the commands that would run
4dvc dag                   # show the stage graph
5dvc metrics show          # current metrics
6dvc metrics diff HEAD     # compare workspace metrics with a commit
7dvc params diff HEAD      # compare parameters

Experiments and cache cleanup

When you are still trying parameters and do not want a commit yet, the experiment commands record a run and leave the workspace as it was:

1dvc exp run -S train.max_depth=6
2dvc exp show
3dvc exp apply <experiment>   # bring that run back into the workspace, then commit it yourself

The local cache grows with every version. dvc gc deletes nothing unless you pass a scope. -w keeps only the objects referenced by the pointers in the current workspace, and drops other versions from the local cache:

1dvc gc -w

Objects you already dvc pushed can be restored later with dvc fetch. --cloud deletes the remote with the same scope. Versions removed there are gone from that remote, so use it only after you are sure the old data can go.

A typical example

The dataset below is for churn prediction. DVC tracks the raw CSV. Split and train are two stages. On another machine, git clone and dvc pull retrieve the same data and the same model.

Repository layout:

1.
2├── data/
3│   └── raw.csv
4├── src/
5│   ├── prepare.py
6│   └── train.py
7├── params.yaml
8├── dvc.yaml
9└── dvc.lock          # written by dvc repro

data/raw.csv needs feature columns and label. These three rows only show the shape. A real file needs enough rows of both labels, or one side of the split will be missing a class:

1tenure,monthly_charges,label
23,29.85,0
312,56.95,0
41,89.10,1

params.yaml:

1prepare:
2  test_size: 0.2
3  seed: 7
4train:
5  max_depth: 4
6  seed: 7

src/prepare.py reads the parameters and the raw data, and writes the two splits:

 1from pathlib import Path
 2
 3import pandas as pd
 4import yaml
 5from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
 6
 7
 8def main():
 9    with open("params.yaml") as f:
10        params = yaml.safe_load(f)["prepare"]
11    df = pd.read_csv("data/raw.csv")
12    train, test = train_test_split(
13        df,
14        test_size=params["test_size"],
15        random_state=params["seed"],
16    )
17    Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
18    train.to_csv("data/train.csv", index=False)
19    test.to_csv("data/test.csv", index=False)
20
21
22if __name__ == "__main__":
23    main()

src/train.py reads the splits and writes the model and the metrics:

 1import json
 2from pathlib import Path
 3
 4import joblib
 5import pandas as pd
 6import yaml
 7from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
 8from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
 9
10
11def main():
12    with open("params.yaml") as f:
13        params = yaml.safe_load(f)["train"]
14    train = pd.read_csv("data/train.csv")
15    test = pd.read_csv("data/test.csv")
16    features = [col for col in train.columns if col != "label"]
17
18    model = DecisionTreeClassifier(
19        max_depth=params["max_depth"],
20        random_state=params["seed"],
21    )
22    model.fit(train[features], train["label"])
23    proba = model.predict_proba(test[features])[:, 1]
24
25    Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
26    joblib.dump(model, "models/model.pkl")
27    Path("metrics.json").write_text(
28        json.dumps({"roc_auc": float(roc_auc_score(test["label"], proba))}, indent=2)
29        + "\n"
30    )
31
32
33if __name__ == "__main__":
34    main()

dvc.yaml:

 1stages:
 2  prepare:
 3    cmd: python src/prepare.py
 4    deps:
 5      - src/prepare.py
 6      - data/raw.csv
 7    params:
 8      - prepare
 9    outs:
10      - data/train.csv
11      - data/test.csv
12  train:
13    cmd: python src/train.py
14    deps:
15      - src/train.py
16      - data/train.csv
17      - data/test.csv
18    params:
19      - train
20    outs:
21      - models/model.pkl
22    metrics:
23      - metrics.json:
24          cache: false

Track the data the first time

 1git init
 2dvc init
 3pip install dvc pandas scikit-learn pyyaml joblib
 4
 5dvc add data/raw.csv
 6git add data/raw.csv.dvc data/.gitignore .dvc
 7git commit -m "track raw dataset with dvc"
 8
 9dvc remote add -d storage /mnt/dvc-storage
10git add .dvc/config
11git commit -m "add dvc remote"
12dvc push

If the Synology NAS is not mounted as a share, use the WebDAV remote from the previous section instead of /mnt/dvc-storage. The git add and dvc push steps stay the same.

At this point Git has the pointer and the remote address, and the remote has the CSV. data/raw.csv does not show up as a file to commit in git status.

Run the pipeline and commit

After the scripts, params.yaml, and dvc.yaml are in place:

1dvc repro
2dvc metrics show

dvc repro runs prepare, then train, and writes dvc.lock. data/train.csv, data/test.csv, and models/model.pkl go into the cache. metrics.json stays in the workspace.

1git add dvc.yaml dvc.lock params.yaml src metrics.json
2git commit -m "add prepare and train stages"
3dvc push
4git push

Both git commit and dvc push have to happen. Pushing only Git tells others the hash, but they cannot fetch the file. Pushing only DVC leaves them without the hash to pull.

Another machine

1git clone git@github.com:org/churn.git
2cd churn
3dvc pull          # fetch raw.csv, the splits, and the model from the lockfile
4dvc repro         # nothing changed, so both stages are skipped

Change a parameter

Set train.max_depth in params.yaml from 4 to 8:

1dvc repro
2dvc metrics diff HEAD
3dvc params diff HEAD

prepare is unchanged, so it is skipped. train sees a new parameter and runs again. After you accept the metrics:

1git add dvc.lock params.yaml metrics.json
2git commit -m "train with max_depth 8"
3dvc push

When the data itself changes, edit data/raw.csv and run dvc add data/raw.csv again. Once the hash changes, dvc repro starts over from prepare.

To compare a few depths before committing:

1dvc exp run -S train.max_depth=6
2dvc exp show

Pick one run, bring it back with dvc exp apply, then commit and dvc push as above.

Return to the previous version

1git checkout HEAD~1
2dvc checkout

Code, parameters, and dvc.lock return to the previous commit, and the CSV and model in the workspace return to that hash. That is the version you get by tying DVC to one Git commit.

Command details are in the DVC Command Reference. Pipeline fields are in dvc.yaml. Get “pointers in Git, contents on the remote, reruns decided by the lockfile” working before you add experiments and cache cleanup.

19    test.to_csv("data/test.csv", index=False)
20
21
22if __name__ == "__main__":
23    main()

 1import json
 2from pathlib import Path
 3
 4import joblib
 5import pandas as pd
 6import yaml
 7from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
 8from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
 9
10
11def main():
12    with open("params.yaml") as f:
13        params = yaml.safe_load(f)["train"]
14    train = pd.read_csv("data/train.csv")
15    test = pd.read_csv("data/test.csv")
16    features = [col for col in train.columns if col != "label"]
17
18    model = DecisionTreeClassifier(
19        max_depth=params["max_depth"],
20        random_state=params["seed"],
21    )
22    model.fit(train[features], train["label"])
23    proba = model.predict_proba(test[features])[:, 1]
24
25    Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
26    joblib.dump(model, "models/model.pkl")
27    Path("metrics.json").write_text(
28        json.dumps({"roc_auc": float(roc_auc_score(test["label"], proba))}, indent=2)
29        + "\n"
30    )
31
32
33if __name__ == "__main__":
34    main()

dvc.yaml:

 1stages:
 2  prepare:
 3    cmd: python src/prepare.py
 4    deps:
 5      - src/prepare.py
 6      - data/raw.csv
 7    params:
 8      - prepare
 9    outs:
10      - data/train.csv
11      - data/test.csv
12  train:
13    cmd: python src/train.py
14    deps:
15      - src/train.py
16      - data/train.csv
17      - data/test.csv
18    params:
19      - train
20    outs:
21      - models/model.pkl
22    metrics:
23      - metrics.json:
24          cache: false

Track the data the first time

 1git init
 2dvc init
 3pip install dvc pandas scikit-learn pyyaml joblib
 4
 5dvc add data/raw.csv
 6git add data/raw.csv.dvc data/.gitignore .dvc
 7git commit -m "track raw dataset with dvc"
 8
 9dvc remote add -d storage /mnt/dvc-storage
10git add .dvc/config
11git commit -m "add dvc remote"
12dvc push

If the Synology NAS is not mounted as a share, use the WebDAV remote from the previous section instead of /mnt/dvc-storage. The git add and dvc push steps stay the same.

At this point Git has the pointer and the remote address, and the remote has the CSV. data/raw.csv does not show up as a file to commit in git status.

Run the pipeline and commit

After the scripts, params.yaml, and dvc.yaml are in place:

1dvc repro
2dvc metrics show

dvc repro runs prepare, then train, and writes dvc.lock. data/train.csv, data/test.csv, and models/model.pkl go into the cache. metrics.json stays in the workspace.

1git add dvc.yaml dvc.lock params.yaml src metrics.json
2git commit -m "add prepare and train stages"
3dvc push
4git push

Both git commit and dvc push have to happen. Pushing only Git tells others the hash, but they cannot fetch the file. Pushing only DVC leaves them without the hash to pull.

Another machine

1git clone git@github.com:org/churn.git
2cd churn
3dvc pull          # fetch raw.csv, the splits, and the model from the lockfile
4dvc repro         # nothing changed, so both stages are skipped

Change a parameter

Set train.max_depth in params.yaml from 4 to 8:

1dvc repro
2dvc metrics diff HEAD
3dvc params diff HEAD

prepare is unchanged, so it is skipped. train sees a new parameter and runs again. After you accept the metrics:

1git add dvc.lock params.yaml metrics.json
2git commit -m "train with max_depth 8"
3dvc push

When the data itself changes, edit data/raw.csv and run dvc add data/raw.csv again. Once the hash changes, dvc repro starts over from prepare.

To compare a few depths before committing:

1dvc exp run -S train.max_depth=6
2dvc exp show

Pick one run, bring it back with dvc exp apply, then commit and dvc push as above.

Return to the previous version

1git checkout HEAD~1
2dvc checkout

Code, parameters, and dvc.lock return to the previous commit, and the CSV and model in the workspace return to that hash. That is the version you get by tying DVC to one Git commit.

Command details are in the DVC Command Reference. Pipeline fields are in dvc.yaml. Get “pointers in Git, contents on the remote, reruns decided by the lockfile” working before you add experiments and cache cleanup.

item.title: How to learn MLOps, in practice
item.author: nb@nbtyfood.com (jobcher)
item.description:
MLOps is the work of making a model trainable by someone else, blocked by evaluation, deployed, observed, and reversible to the previous version when it goes wrong.

If you already know Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD, what is missing is wiring data, experiments, and models into that delivery path. The stages below start from there. If your background is algorithms or data analysis, replace stage 0 with the engineering gap (Git, tests, Docker, one scheduler). The later stages stay the same.

How MLOps maps onto the ops you already do

A model path usually looks like this:

data in → validation and features → training → offline evaluation → model registry → deploy → online inference → watch drift and outcomes → decide whether to retrain

What you already do What you also have to manage for a model
Code versions Code, data, and model versions that line up
Building an image The image also pins the model artifact and the feature transformer
Unit tests Add data checks and offline evaluation, and fail the pipeline when they miss the bar
Release and rollback Move the model alias from staging to production; rollback points the alias at the previous version
CPU, error rate, latency Also watch input distribution, prediction distribution, and business metrics that arrive late

A complete platform is still a broken path if you cannot answer which data, which code, and which image produced the model that is serving traffic.

Stage 0: the smallest machine-learning set (2–4 weeks)

The goal is to read training code, read metrics, and decide whether two experiments can be compared. You do not need to start with papers.

What to learn:

  • How to split training, validation, and test. Information from the validation set must not leak into features or preprocessing.
  • Common metrics for classification and regression: precision, recall, F1, AUC, MAE, RMSE. When classes are extremely imbalanced, accuracy is almost useless.
  • When overfitting, underfitting, regularization, and early stopping show up.
  • Missing values, categorical encoding, and numeric scaling. A transformer fitted at training time must be used unchanged at inference time.
  • One tabular model with scikit-learn or XGBoost: read data, train, print metrics, save the model to a file.
  • A command-line script as the training entry point. Fix the random seed. Put parameters in a config file.

Done when: you pick a public tabular dataset (UCI Adult is fine) and write train.py. The command line takes a data path and a config. When it finishes, you have metrics and a model file.

Stay with tabular models in this stage. Backprop derivations, paper reading, and large-model fine-tuning come after the path actually runs.

Stage 1: one experiment that someone else can reproduce (3–4 weeks)

After someone clones the repo, they can rerun the same experiment. That is the first brick of MLOps.

Use Python, Git, MLflow, and DVC.

  • Use venv or uv, and lock dependency versions.
  • Do not commit data or model files. DVC commits only the pointer file. Large files live in remote storage.
  • Each training run records parameters, metrics, and the model with MLflow Tracking.
  • One experiment is one YAML config.
  • Cover feature transforms with pytest. Leave a small-sample smoke test on the training script so the command can finish.

These commands should be stable when you check the stage off:

1dvc pull
2python train.py --config conf/baseline.yaml
3mlflow ui

Run again with a different parameter set. The two MLflow runs can be compared side by side. On another machine, git clone followed by dvc pull reproduces the metrics.

Stage 2: turn the script into a pipeline (3–4 weeks)

A pipeline is something that can be scheduled, retried, and rerun from an intermediate step. Split it in this order:

  1. Validate raw data: field types, null ratios, value ranges.
  2. Split the dataset, and version the split on its own.
  3. Fit the feature transform, and save the transformer with the model.
  4. Train.
  5. Evaluate on the held-out set. If the score is below a threshold written down in advance, the process exits non-zero.
  6. Only after evaluation passes, register the model and assign the staging alias.

Pick one orchestrator. To move fast, chain the steps with a Makefile or a short Python script. To match an existing scheduler, use Airflow or Prefect. Kubeflow Pipelines fits a team that already runs Kubernetes and is ready to standardize a training platform. It is a poor first orchestration course.

Hook CI to the GitLab CI or GitHub Actions you already have. Every push runs lint, pytest, and the small-sample smoke test. A full training run happens on a tag or a manual trigger.

 1stages: [test, train]
 2
 3test:
 4  stage: test
 5  script:
 6    - pip install -r requirements.txt
 7    - pytest
 8
 9train:
10  stage: train
11  when: manual
12  script:
13    - dvc pull
14    - python src/train.py --config conf/baseline.yaml
15    - python src/evaluate_gate.py   # exit non-zero below the threshold

Register models with MLflow Model Registry aliases, and load them as models:/churn@production. Promotion points the production alias at the new version. Rollback points it back at the old one. An alias is harder to get wrong than a version number written into the deploy config.

Done when: changing one line of feature code still lets CI finish; when evaluation is below the threshold, the pipeline fails and the production alias does not move.

Stage 3: a service something else can call (3–4 weeks)

Start with online inference. The feedback is fastest. Offline batch scoring is another entry point to the same model. Add it after the interface is stable.

The service does three things: load the model and the transformer at startup, transform features per request, and return a prediction. Load at process start, not on every request.

 1from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
 2
 3import joblib
 4import mlflow.pyfunc
 5import pandas as pd
 6from fastapi import FastAPI
 7from pydantic import BaseModel
 8
 9MODEL_URI = "models:/churn@production"
10
11
12class PredictRequest(BaseModel):
13    tenure: int
14    monthly_charges: float
15    contract: str
16
17    def to_frame(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
18        return pd.DataFrame([self.model_dump()])
19
20
21class State:
22    model = None
23    transformer = None
24
25
26state = State()
27
28
29@asynccontextmanager
30async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
31    state.model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(MODEL_URI)
32    state.transformer = joblib.load("artifacts/transformer.joblib")
33    yield
34
35
36app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
37
38
39@app.post("/predict")
40def predict(req: PredictRequest):
41    features = state.transformer.transform(req.to_frame())
42    proba = state.model.predict(features)
43    return {"proba": float(proba[0]), "model": MODEL_URI}

Then add the things production always runs into:

  • Fix request and response fields with Pydantic. Reject extra fields and missing fields immediately.
  • Put model_version and a request id on the logs. Otherwise you cannot tell which version answered.
  • /health means the model has finished loading. Hand /metrics to Prometheus.
  • Pack it as an image. docker run locally should be enough to get a prediction.
  • FastAPI is enough for a tabular model. For large-model inference on GPUs, look at NVIDIA Triton.

Deploy the way you already deploy on Kubernetes: one Deployment and one Service. Leave KServe until the number of models justifies a shared inference plane.

Done when: the same sample gets the same prediction from the offline script and from the API. The image tag, the model alias, and the transformer file all refer to the same release.

Stage 4: monitoring and rollback (3–4 weeks)

After launch, a model often gets worse while the process stays healthy. The predictions just drift. Watch four layers:

  • Service: QPS, latency, error rate. Prometheus and Grafana, the same stack as the other services.
  • Input: missing-feature rate, mean, quantiles. Compare with the training set or with last week.
  • Output: the distribution of prediction scores, and the share of the positive class. If the shape jumps, check upstream data first.
  • Outcome: when labels arrive late, wait until they are in before computing the real metric. If there are no labels, use a business proxy such as rejection rate or manual-review rate.

Drift can start as a daily job. Compare today’s request sample with the training sample using PSI or Evidently, and send the result to a daily report or a metric. The first bar is one comparison every day.

Release in increasing order of risk:

  1. Replace all traffic, and keep the previous Deployment. If it goes wrong, roll the production alias and the image back together.
  2. Shadow traffic: the new model only records predictions. It does not answer the user.
  3. Split traffic by percentage: 1% → 10% → 100%. At each step, watch latency and the output distribution.

Automatic retraining comes after the gate, the data window, and rollback are all stable. If the trigger is vague, bad data walks straight into the next model.

Done when: you deliberately change the distribution of one feature, and a report or dashboard points at it within a day. After you roll back, the model version in the live logs is the previous one.

Stage 5: a platform, after there are many models

One person or a small group only needs one path through stages 1 to 4. The items below show up when the number of models and the number of people grow:

  • Training and online serving share the same feature computation, so one sample does not produce two different results. The first step is shipping the transformer with the model. A feature store such as Feast comes in when that convention no longer holds.
  • GPU queues and quotas on the cluster. If you already have Kubernetes, attach Kueue or Volcano to the cluster you have.
  • Lineage: a production model traces back to a data version, a Git commit, and an image digest.
  • Permission: who can move an alias to production, and an audit record of that action.
  • If the direction is large language models, add LLMOps: versioned prompts and eval sets, RAG index updates, and cost and latency per request. Underneath, it is still versions, gates, deployment, and monitoring.

Stick to one stack

Keep one tool per step, and learn it well enough to debug it.

Step Learn this Add something else when
Experiments and registry MLflow The team has already standardized on another platform
Data versions DVC Data is in a lake and you need branches and permissions; then look at lakeFS
Pipelines Airflow or Prefect Training jobs already all run on Kubernetes; then evaluate Kubeflow
Serving FastAPI + Docker Large-model inference on GPUs; then Triton
Runtime Kubernetes + the CI you have Many models; then KServe
Monitoring Prometheus + Grafana; drift with PSI or Evidently A daily report is no longer enough; then look at a dedicated model-monitoring product
Cloud Pick one of SageMaker, Vertex AI, or Azure Machine Learning After the open-source path runs, see which piece the managed service removes

Pick the cloud platform that matches the job. Run the path on your own machine first, then look at the managed service. A model clicked together in a console is hard to debug, because you no longer know what you deployed.

Tie it together with one project

The topic can be small. Churn, ticket classification, or credit default all work. The repo ends up with:

 1conf/baseline.yaml          # one config per experiment
 2src/train.py
 3src/features.py
 4src/serve.py
 5src/evaluate_gate.py        # fail below the threshold
 6tests/
 7Dockerfile
 8.gitlab-ci.yml
 9monitoring/drift.py         # daily input comparison
10artifacts/*.dvc             # pointers to data and models, not the files
11README.md

The README covers three things: how to reproduce a given experiment, how to promote a model to production, and how to roll it back.

On a resume this can read: built the train, register, serve, and rollback path for a tabular model; managed the live version with MLflow aliases; blocked release in CI when evaluation missed the bar; ran a daily check for input drift.

How to schedule the time

At 8–10 hours a week:

  • Month 1: stages 0 and 1. You have a training repo someone else can reproduce.
  • Month 2: stages 2 and 3. A pipeline, a registry, and a service that can be called.
  • Month 3: stage 4. Monitoring, drift, rollback, and a finished README.
  • After that: keep the path alive at work and in this repo, then add one cloud platform or GPU inference for the role you want.

If Kubernetes and CI are already familiar, stage 3 goes much faster. Most of the time goes to stages 0 and 1. Skip those and the later platform has nothing to host.

Four things you should be able to explain in an interview

A tool list does not help much. Prepare examples around “the model broke; how did you notice, and what did you do”:

  • A training run no longer matches a historical metric. How you found that the data split or a dependency version had changed.
  • Live quality drops. How you tell apart a service failure, input drift, and a change in the labels themselves.
  • Evaluation fails. Why that model never reaches production.
  • On rollback, whether the image, the model alias, the feature transformer, and the config all go back together.

What to read, in order

  1. Chip Huyen, Designing Machine Learning Systems. Read the data, training, deployment, and monitoring chapters first, and use the book as a map.
  2. MLOps Zoomcamp. Free. The assignments are a path you can actually run.
  3. DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Machine Learning Engineering for Production. Use it to line up the vocabulary.
  4. Tracking and Model Registry in the MLflow docs, plus Get Started with DVC. Do the steps against your own repo.
  5. Google’s Practitioners Guide to MLOps. See how a mature team stages the process.

Papers and framework release notes can wait until this path already runs.

Ways the path gets longer than it needs to be

  • Spending the time on a Kubernetes certification while the repo still has no reproducible training entry point. The cluster is where the model runs.
  • Learning three tools each for experiment tracking, registry, and deployment, and ending with none that can finish a release alone.
  • Notebooks only. Training that CI cannot invoke cannot enter a pipeline.
  • Building automatic retraining and a feature platform before versions, an evaluation gate, and rollback exist. Automation amplifies the mistake.
  • Reporting training-set metrics only, and never checking that the same sample gets the same prediction from the live API.

First make one model retrainable, rejectable, observable, and rollback-able. Once those four exist, a platform and a team standard have something to land on.

Cloud Pick one of SageMaker, Vertex AI, or Azure Machine Learning After the open-source path runs, see which piece the managed service removes

Pick the cloud platform that matches the job. Run the path on your own machine first, then look at the managed service. A model clicked together in a console is hard to debug, because you no longer know what you deployed.

Tie it together with one project

The topic can be small. Churn, ticket classification, or credit default all work. The repo ends up with:

 1conf/baseline.yaml          # one config per experiment
 2src/train.py
 3src/features.py
 4src/serve.py
 5src/evaluate_gate.py        # fail below the threshold
 6tests/
 7Dockerfile
 8.gitlab-ci.yml
 9monitoring/drift.py         # daily input comparison
10artifacts/*.dvc             # pointers to data and models, not the files
11README.md

The README covers three things: how to reproduce a given experiment, how to promote a model to production, and how to roll it back.

On a resume this can read: built the train, register, serve, and rollback path for a tabular model; managed the live version with MLflow aliases; blocked release in CI when evaluation missed the bar; ran a daily check for input drift.

How to schedule the time

At 8–10 hours a week:

  • Month 1: stages 0 and 1. You have a training repo someone else can reproduce.
  • Month 2: stages 2 and 3. A pipeline, a registry, and a service that can be called.
  • Month 3: stage 4. Monitoring, drift, rollback, and a finished README.
  • After that: keep the path alive at work and in this repo, then add one cloud platform or GPU inference for the role you want.

If Kubernetes and CI are already familiar, stage 3 goes much faster. Most of the time goes to stages 0 and 1. Skip those and the later platform has nothing to host.

Four things you should be able to explain in an interview

A tool list does not help much. Prepare examples around “the model broke; how did you notice, and what did you do”:

  • A training run no longer matches a historical metric. How you found that the data split or a dependency version had changed.
  • Live quality drops. How you tell apart a service failure, input drift, and a change in the labels themselves.
  • Evaluation fails. Why that model never reaches production.
  • On rollback, whether the image, the model alias, the feature transformer, and the config all go back together.

What to read, in order

  1. Chip Huyen, Designing Machine Learning Systems. Read the data, training, deployment, and monitoring chapters first, and use the book as a map.
  2. MLOps Zoomcamp. Free. The assignments are a path you can actually run.
  3. DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Machine Learning Engineering for Production. Use it to line up the vocabulary.
  4. Tracking and Model Registry in the MLflow docs, plus Get Started with DVC. Do the steps against your own repo.
  5. Google’s Practitioners Guide to MLOps. See how a mature team stages the process.

Papers and framework release notes can wait until this path already runs.

Ways the path gets longer than it needs to be

  • Spending the time on a Kubernetes certification while the repo still has no reproducible training entry point. The cluster is where the model runs.
  • Learning three tools each for experiment tracking, registry, and deployment, and ending with none that can finish a release alone.
  • Notebooks only. Training that CI cannot invoke cannot enter a pipeline.
  • Building automatic retraining and a feature platform before versions, an evaluation gate, and rollback exist. Automation amplifies the mistake.
  • Reporting training-set metrics only, and never checking that the same sample gets the same prediction from the live API.

First make one model retrainable, rejectable, observable, and rollback-able. Once those four exist, a platform and a team standard have something to land on.

Welcome to Jobcher’s Blog

Welcome to my personal blog! This is a space where I share my thoughts, experiences, and knowledge about technology, software development, Kubernetes, and more.

About This Blog

This blog covers various topics including:

  • Kubernetes and Container Orchestration: Tutorials, best practices, and deployment guides
  • DevOps and CI/CD: Automation, infrastructure as code, and deployment strategies
  • Software Development: Programming languages, frameworks, and development tools
  • System Administration: Linux, networking, and system optimization
  • Technology Insights: Reviews, comparisons, and industry trends

What to Expect

You’ll find practical guides, tutorials, and insights based on real-world experiences. Most articles are currently available in Chinese, but I’m working on providing more English content.
